title: Venus et Adonis. Atalanta
titleEn: The Golden Apples and the Death of Adonis — Metamorphoses X.636–739
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Venus tells Adonis how she answered Hippomenes' prayer: three golden apples picked in her own Cyprian field, thrown one by one to pull Atalanta out of her stride, and a race won by the man she helped. He gave her neither thanks nor incense, so she drove him to lie with Atalanta in a holy hollow beside a temple of the Mother of the gods, who turned the pair into the lions that champ her bit. Venus warns Adonis away from every animal that stands and fights; he hunts a boar anyway and dies of it, and she sprinkles nectar on his blood and raises from it a flower the wind shakes down.

sentences.t:
Dixerat; utque rudis primoque Cupidine tacta,
quid facit ignorans, amat et non sentit amorem.
sentences.l: She had spoken; and, as one untried and touched by a first Cupid, not knowing what she is doing, she loves and does not feel the love.
sentences.i: She had finished; and green as she was, touched by a first Cupid, with no idea what she is doing, she loves and does not perceive that it is love.
sentences.n: The pluperfect dixerat, “she had finished speaking”, closes a speech, and the feminine participle tacta shows the speaker was the girl. Everything from here to the end of 707 is spoken by Venus, telling Adonis the story of Atalanta and Hippomenes: the first person from 639 onwards is hers. Her telling sits inside a longer song — the quotation mark that closes 739 shuts a quotation opened before these lines. utque is et ut, “and as”; rudis is “without experience”. quid facit ignorans is an indirect question governed by the participle, with a present tense inside a past frame, so English wants “what she is doing”. Cupido is the god's name standing for the thing he causes. Magnus prints quid, “what”; the second witness prints quod, which turns the phrase into a relative, “ignorant of the thing she does”. The weight of the line is on sentit: she has the love and does not recognise it for what it is.

sentences.t:
Iam solitos poscunt cursus populusque paterque,
cum me sollicita proles Neptunia voce
invocat Hippomenes “Cytherea” que “comprecor, ausis
adsit” ait “nostris et quos dedit adiuvet ignes.”
sentences.l: Now the people and the father are demanding the customary races, when Hippomenes, Neptune's offspring, calls upon me with an anxious voice, and “Cytherea,” he says, “I pray: let her stand by the daring we have undertaken, and let her help the fires she herself gave.”
sentences.i: Now the crowd and her father were calling for the usual race, when Hippomenes, Neptune's descendant, called on me with the strain in his voice: “Cytherea,” he said, “this is my prayer — may she stand beside what I dare, and help on the fires she herself gave.”
sentences.n: cum with the present invocat after the present poscunt keeps the whole scene in the historic present. proles Neptunia, “Neptune's offspring”, names Hippomenes by descent before the name arrives. The prayer is in the third person throughout — comprecor governs the jussive subjunctives adsit and adiuvet — while the goddess herself is named in the vocative: the ordinary Latin manner of praying aloud, naming the god and then speaking of her rather than to her, which is why the English keeps “let her”. ausis is the dative of the neuter noun ausum, “a thing dared”, with adsit; nostris is the plural of a single speaker, one man praying for himself. quos dedit ignes is a relative clause with its antecedent drawn inside it, “the fires which she gave”, ignes being the fires of love. The edition sets the enclitic -que outside its quotation mark, so a bare que stands in the line; it joins invocat to ait, “calls on me … and says”.

sentences.t:
Detulit aura preces ad me non invida blandas;
motaque sum, fateor. Nec opis mora longa dabatur.
sentences.l: A breeze, not grudging, carried the coaxing prayers down to me; and I was moved, I confess. Nor was a long delay of help being granted.
sentences.i: The air was not grudging: it brought his coaxing prayer down to me, and I was moved — I admit it. And the help was not long in coming.
sentences.n: preces is pulled a long way from its adjective blandas, which is held back to the end of the line with the breeze, the goddess and the litotes shut between them; blandus is the adjective of coaxing, wheedling speech, the language of a lover. non invida is understatement of the standard Latin kind: not “not grudging” as a fact about winds but “obliging”. fateor, “I confess it”, is Venus interrupting her own story to the young man listening. opis is a genitive with mora, “delay of help”, and dabatur is imperfect passive, so the negative covers the whole stretch of time rather than a single moment.

sentences.t:
Est ager, indigenae Tamasenum nomine dicunt,
telluris Cypriae pars optima, quam mihi prisci
sacravere senes templisque accedere dotem
hanc iussere meis.
sentences.l: There is a field — the native people call it by the name Tamasene — the best part of the Cyprian land, which men of old consecrated to me and ordered this ground to be added as an endowment to my temples.
sentences.i: There is a field, Tamasene by the name its own people give it, the finest part of the Cyprian country: the old men of an earlier age made it holy to me, and ordered it to go with my temples as their endowment.
sentences.n: sacravere and iussere are sacraverunt and iusserunt, the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere, which runs through this poem and gets no more than a reminder hereafter. Tamasenum is accusative, predicative after dicunt with nomine, the field itself being left unexpressed as the object — “they call it Tamasene by name”. accedere dotem hanc is an accusative and infinitive after iussere, with dotem predicative — a dos is the property that goes with a bride, so the field is spoken of as the temples' marriage portion. templis meis is the dative accedere takes. Magnus prints quam, agreeing with pars, “the best part … which”; the second witness prints quem, which attaches the relative to ager instead. The sense is the same either way.

sentences.t:
Medio nitet arbor in arvo,
fulva comas, fulvo ramis crepitantibus auro.
sentences.l: In the middle of the field a tree shines, tawny as to its foliage, with its branches rattling with tawny gold.
sentences.i: In the middle of that field a tree stands shining, its leaves tawny, its branches rattling with tawny gold.
sentences.n: comas is a Greek accusative of respect after the adjective fulva: the tree is tawny not all over but with regard to its hair, which is what comae are before they are leaves. This construction — an accusative telling you in what respect something is true — recurs constantly in the poem. The two fulv- words open the second line with only comas between them, one of the leaves and one of the metal, and fulvo is then held apart from its auro to the end of the line; crepitare is the verb of a dry rattle, so the tree is heard as well as seen.

sentences.t:
Hinc tria forte mea veniens decerpta ferebam
aurea poma manu:
sentences.l: From here, as I was coming, I happened to be carrying three golden apples, plucked with my own hand:
sentences.i: I was on my way from there and happened to have with me three golden apples I had picked myself:
sentences.n: forte, “by chance”, goes with ferebam — she happened to be carrying them — and the chance is Venus's own word for it. decerpta is a perfect passive participle agreeing with poma, “having been picked”. mea and manu are split across the line-end, mea standing in the middle of 649 and manu in 650, so the hand she picked them with arrives a line after the possessive that claims it.

sentences.t:
nullique videnda nisi ipsi
Hippomenen adii docuique, quis usus in illis.
sentences.l: and, to be seen by no one but himself, I approached Hippomenes and taught him what use there was in them.
sentences.i: and, visible to no one but him, I came up to Hippomenes and showed him what they were for.
sentences.n: videnda is a gerundive with nulli … nisi ipsi as its dative of agent: literally “to be seen by no one except him”, which is how Latin says that a god shows herself to one person only. adii is the perfect of adeo, whose object is the person approached. docui takes two accusatives, the person taught and the thing taught, and here the thing is the indirect question quis usus in illis, with the verb left out — “what use there was in them”.

sentences.t:
Signa tubae dederant, cum carcere pronus uterque
emicat et summam celeri pede libat harenam.
sentences.l: The trumpets had given the signals, when both of them, leaning forward, dart out from the starting-box and just touch the top of the sand with a swift foot.
sentences.i: The trumpets had sounded, when the two of them shot out of the stalls, each leaning into it, their quick feet barely grazing the surface of the sand.
sentences.n: A pluperfect followed by cum and the present is the construction grammars call cum inversum: the subordinate clause carries the main event and the sentence turns over on it. carcer is the barrier or stall a racer starts from. uterque, “each of the two”, takes singular verbs, emicat and libat, though two people are running. libare is properly to take a sip of a thing or pour a first offering of it, so the foot is said to taste the sand rather than tread it; summam harenam is “the topmost sand”, the surface only.

sentences.t:
Posse putes illos sicco freta radere passu
et segetis canae stantes percurrere aristas.
sentences.l: You would think that they could shave the sea with a dry step and run across the standing ears of a whitening cornfield.
sentences.i: You would think they could cross open water and keep their feet dry, and run along the tops of a standing crop.
sentences.n: putes is a potential subjunctive with an indefinite second person, “one would think”, and it governs the accusative and infinitive posse illos. radere is to scrape or shave, used of a keel taking a shoreline closely; freta are the straits or open water. segetis canae is a genitive of the whitening crop, with stantes aristas its standing ears — the point being that nothing is bent. This pairing of two impossibilities is the standard way of putting speed beyond measurement.

sentences.t:
Adiciunt animos iuveni clamorque favorque
verbaque dicentum:
sentences.l: Shouting and support and the words of those calling out add spirit to the young man:
sentences.i: The noise and the backing and the words of the crowd put heart into the young man:
sentences.n: animos adicere is “to add spirit”, with iuveni as the dative of the person it is added to; animus in the plural is courage rather than mind. The three -que endings string the subjects together without a pause, which is the sound of a crowd. dicentum is dicentium, the shorter genitive plural of the present participle that verse prefers; it has no noun, so the participle itself supplies “of those speaking”.

sentences.t:
“Nunc, nunc incumbere tempus!
Hippomene, propera! nunc viribus utere totis!
pelle moram, vinces!”
sentences.l: “Now, now is the time to lean into it! Hippomenes, hurry! now use all your strength! Drive off delay — you will win!”
sentences.i: “Now, now is the moment to press! Hippomenes, go! use everything you have! Away with holding back — you will win!”
sentences.n: tempus stands with est understood and the infinitive incumbere depending on it: incumbere is to lean one's weight onto a thing, the word for putting the body into an effort. Hippomene is a Greek vocative, keeping its Greek ending in Latin verse. utere is the imperative of the deponent utor, which takes an ablative, viribus totis. vinces is a plain future indicative used as encouragement — not “you may win” but “you will”, which is what a crowd shouts.

sentences.t:
Dubium, Megareius heros
gaudeat, an virgo magis his Schoeneia dictis.
sentences.l: A doubtful thing, whether the hero of Megareus' line takes more delight in these words, or the maiden, Schoeneus' daughter.
sentences.i: It is hard to say which of the two was the more pleased by this — Megareus' son, or Schoeneus' daughter.
sentences.n: dubium is a bare neuter adjective with est left out, and English has to supply “it is uncertain”. What follows is a double indirect question with the first limb unmarked and an introducing the second, so gaudeat is subjunctive; his dictis is the ablative of the thing one is glad about. magis belongs to both limbs at once. Megareius and Schoeneia are adjectives built on a father's name, Megareus and Schoeneus, the ordinary verse alternative to saying whose son and whose daughter. Megareius could be read instead as “of Megara”, but the pairing with Schoeneia tells against that, and so does proles Neptunia at 639 and 665: in the genealogy Megareus is himself Neptune's son, which is what makes Hippomenes Neptune's offspring.

sentences.t:
O quotiens, cum iam posset transire, morata est
spectatosque diu vultus invita reliquit!
sentences.l: Oh, how often, when she might already have gone past, she hung back, and unwilling left behind the face she had long been gazing at!
sentences.i: How often, when she could have gone by him, she held back — and left behind, against her will, the face she had been looking at so long!
sentences.n: quotiens with an exclamation counts the times without naming a number. posset is imperfect subjunctive in a cum clause of circumstance, and transire is the technical word of the race, to overtake. morata est is the perfect of the deponent moror, active in sense: she delayed herself. invita is a nominative adjective where English wants an adverbial phrase — Latin says what she was, “unwilling”, and lets it colour the verb. spectatos diu vultus is “the face long looked at”, plural for singular as vultus regularly is.

sentences.t:
Aridus e lasso veniebat anhelitus ore,
metaque erat longe.
sentences.l: A dry gasping was coming from the weary mouth, and the turning-post was far off.
sentences.i: Dry, gasping breath came out of the tired mouth, and the post was still a long way off.
sentences.n: There is no possessive with ore: the Latin says only “from the weary mouth”, and it is the next sentence, in which Hippomenes throws the first apple, that points to the mouth being his. aridus is dry in the throat, the panting of someone whose breath has stopped being easy. meta is the post at the end or the turn of a racecourse, the mark the runners make for.

sentences.t:
Tum denique de tribus unum
fetibus arboreis proles Neptunia misit.
sentences.l: Then at last, of the three tree-fruits, Neptune's offspring let one fly.
sentences.i: Then at last, of the three fruits from that tree, Neptune's descendant threw one.
sentences.n: de tribus fetibus is a partitive de with the ablative where earlier Latin would use a genitive; it is ordinary in verse. fetus is what a thing brings forth, used of a woman's child as readily as of a tree's crop, so the line sets one word for offspring against another: the fruits are the tree's fetus and the thrower is Neptune's proles. misit is the plain verb for letting a missile go.

sentences.t:
Obstipuit virgo, nitidique cupidine pomi
declinat cursus aurumque volubile tollit.
sentences.l: The maiden was stunned, and in her desire for the shining apple she turns her course aside and lifts the rolling gold.
sentences.i: The girl stopped short, and wanting the shining apple she swerved from her line and picked up the gold as it rolled.
sentences.n: obstipuit is a perfect, and then declinat and tollit are presents: the shock is reported as a completed fact and the two actions it causes are put in front of the reader as they happen. cupidine is an ablative of cause. declinat cursus has the accusative plural of cursus for the single run she is making, plural for singular again. volubile is the adjective of a thing that can roll, so the gold is still moving when she takes it.

sentences.t: Praeterit Hippomenes! Resonant spectacula plausu.
sentences.l: Hippomenes goes past! The stands ring with applause.
sentences.i: Hippomenes is past her! The banked seats ring with the clapping.
sentences.n: Two short sentences, five words between them and both in the present, are the whole of the moment. spectacula is the word for a show used of the place a show is watched from, the tiers of seats; plausu is the ablative of the sound the ringing is made of.

sentences.t:
Illa moram celeri cessataque tempora cursu
corrigit atque iterum iuvenem post terga relinquit.
sentences.l: She makes good the delay and the time idled away, with a swift run, and again leaves the young man behind her back.
sentences.i: With a burst of speed she makes up the pause and the time she wasted, and once more leaves the young man behind her.
sentences.n: corrigit governs both moram and cessata tempora, and celeri cursu is the ablative of the means she does it by, its two words split around the second of them. cessata is a passive participle made from cesso, a verb that has no object of its own — verse allows it and English has to say “the time that was idled”. post terga, “behind her back”, is plural for singular.

sentences.t:
Et rursus pomi iactu remorata secundi
consequitur transitque virum.
sentences.l: And, held up again by the throwing of a second apple, she catches the man up and goes past him.
sentences.i: Held up again by the throw of a second apple, she caught him and passed him.
sentences.n: remorata is the perfect participle of the deponent remoror, and such a participle can be used either way: “having delayed herself” or “having been delayed”. Here the ablative iactu, the throw that held her up, points to the second, and the literal follows it. pomi and secundi belong together but are pulled apart, with iactu remorata standing between them and secundi held to the end of the line. consequitur and transit are two stages of one movement, coming level and then going by, and virum, “the man”, is the only word for Hippomenes here.

sentences.t:
Pars ultima cursus
restabat; “nunc” inquit “ades, dea muneris auctor!”
sentences.l: The last part of the course was left; “now,” he says, “be at hand, goddess, giver of the gift!”
sentences.i: The last stretch of the course was left. “Now,” he said, “be here, goddess — you gave the gift!”
sentences.n: restabat is imperfect, the state of things when he speaks. ades is the imperative of adsum and the standing cult word for a god's being present where she is wanted; a Roman prayer asks for that before it asks for anything else. dea and auctor are both vocatives in apposition, auctor being the maker or originator of a thing and used here of a woman without changing its ending. This prayer speaks to Venus in the second person, unlike the one at 640, where he named her and then prayed of her in the third.

sentences.t:
inque latus campi, quo tardius illa rediret,
iecit ab obliquo nitidum iuvenaliter aurum.
sentences.l: and off to the side of the field, so that she might come back the more slowly, he threw the shining gold from a slant, in the manner of a young man.
sentences.i: and out to the side of the field — so that her way back would take longer — he flung the shining gold away at an angle, with a young man's arm behind it.
sentences.n: quo with a comparative, tardius, is a purpose clause: quo stands for ut eo, “so that by that much”, and rediret is its subjunctive. ab obliquo is an adverbial phrase built on a neuter adjective, “from the slanting”, that is, not straight down the course. iuvenaliter is a rare adverb from iuvenalis, and it carries both the strength of a young man's throw and the showing off in it.

sentences.t:
An peteret, virgo visa est dubitare: coegi
tollere et adieci sublato pondera malo
impediique oneris pariter gravitate moraque.
sentences.l: Whether she should go after it, the maiden seemed to hesitate: I compelled her to pick it up, and I put weight into the apple once it was raised, and I hindered her alike by the heaviness of the load and by the delay.
sentences.i: The girl seemed to hesitate whether to go after it. I made her pick it up; and once it was in her hand I put weight into it, and held her back by the load and by the time it cost, both at once.
sentences.n: an peteret is an indirect question standing in front of the verb that governs it, dubitare, which is why English has to turn the order round. coegi has tollere with no object expressed. sublato malo can be read as a dative with adieci, “to the apple, once it had been lifted”, or as an ablative absolute, “the apple having been lifted”; the sense is the same and the ambiguity costs nothing. malum, “apple”, has a long first vowel and is a different word from malum, “an evil”, with a short one; the edition prints no vowel lengths. The two ablatives at the end are held together by pariter and the -que, one physical and one temporal.

sentences.t:
Neve meus sermo cursu sit tardior ipso,
praeterita est virgo: duxit sua praemia victor.
sentences.l: And so that my own telling should not be slower than the race itself: the maiden was passed; the winner led away his prize.
sentences.i: And not to let my telling run slower than the race itself — the girl was passed, and the winner led away what he had won.
sentences.n: neve with the subjunctive sit is a negative purpose clause with no main clause of its own to depend on: Venus breaks off her own story to say why she is cutting it short. sermo is talk or telling, and cursu ipso is the ablative of comparison after tardior. duxit is the verb used of a man taking a bride home, so praemia, plural for singular, is the girl herself; the sentence says what the race was for without saying it.

sentences.t:
Dignane, cui grates ageret, cui turis honorem
ferret, Adoni, fui? —
sentences.l: Was I worthy, Adonis — one to whom he should render thanks, to whom he should bring the honour of incense?
sentences.i: Had I not earned it, Adonis — thanks from him, the honour of incense?
sentences.n: dignane is dignus with the question particle -ne attached. The two cui clauses are relative clauses of the kind Latin puts in the subjunctive after dignus, ageret and ferret: not “to whom he gave thanks” but “the sort of person thanks should be given to”. grates agere is the fixed phrase for thanks rendered to a god, as distinct from the ordinary gratias agere between people. Adoni is a Greek vocative: Venus turns from her story to the young man beside her and puts the question to him, though she does not wait for an answer from him.

sentences.t:
nec grates inmemor egit,
nec mihi tura dedit.
sentences.l: — he rendered no thanks, forgetful as he was, nor did he give me incense.
sentences.i: — no: he forgot, and gave me neither thanks nor incense.
sentences.n: Venus answers her own question, and the edition marks the turn with a dash. inmemor is the edition's spelling of immemor and is a nominative adjective doing the work of a clause: “being unmindful”, which English can carry either as “forgetful as he was” or as a verb of its own. The two nec clauses take back the two things asked for in the question just before, thanks and incense, in the same order.

sentences.l: I am turned into sudden anger; and, smarting at the contempt, so that I should not be one to be scorned by those to come, I take precaution by an example, and I myself urge myself on against the pair of them.
sentences.i: All at once I turn to anger; and stung by the slight, so that later ages should not think me a goddess who can be despised, I guard against that by making an example, and rouse myself against them both.
sentences.n: convertor is passive in form but middle in force: she turns, and no one turns her. The literal keeps the Latin's passive shape and the idiomatic gives the sense. contemptu is an ablative of cause with dolens. ne sim spernenda is a gerundive in a negative purpose clause — “that I may not be a thing that has to be scorned” — with futuris, “those who will be”, as its dative of agent. exemplo is the ablative of the means she takes precaution by, and the example is what the rest of her story describes. meque ipsa has me as the object and ipsa in the nominative, agreeing with the speaker.

sentences.t:
Templa, deum Matri quae quondam clarus Echion
fecerat ex voto, nemorosis abdita silvis,
transibant, et iter longum requiescere suasit.
sentences.l: They were passing a temple which famous Echion had once made for the Mother of the gods out of a vow, hidden away in wooded forest; and the long road persuaded them to rest.
sentences.i: They were passing a shrine that Echion, a man of note, had built long before for the Mother of the gods to discharge a vow, hidden deep in woodland; and the long road made resting seem good.
sentences.n: Templa is plural for singular, as Latin regularly is with a building of this kind, and abdita agrees with it. deum is deorum, the shorter genitive plural that verse keeps and the edition prints. ex voto is the standing phrase for a thing built to pay off a promise made to a god; the Mother of the gods is Cybele, named by her adjective at 704. suasit has the infinitive requiescere with no subject expressed, so the persuading is done to nobody in particular — the road persuades, and English supplies “them”.

sentences.t:
Illic concubitus intempestiva cupido
occupat Hippomenen, a numine concita nostro.
sentences.l: There an untimely desire for lying together takes hold of Hippomenes, roused by my own divine power.
sentences.i: There a desire to lie with her takes Hippomenes at the wrong moment — a desire that my own godhead had stirred.
sentences.n: concubitus is a genitive with cupido, the desire being for the thing named. intempestiva is “out of due season”, and it covers the moment and the place at once. concita is feminine and agrees with cupido, not with Hippomenen, though the word order puts it next to the man — the desire is what was stirred up. a numine nostro is Venus's own claim, made in her own voice to the young man listening: she says she caused what follows, and the poem has no other authority for it than her.

sentences.t:
Luminis exigui fuerat prope templa recessus,
speluncae similis, nativo pumice tectus,
religione sacer prisca,
sentences.l: There had been near the temple a recess of scant light, like a cave, roofed with pumice as it grew, holy with an ancient religious awe,
sentences.i: Near the shrine was a hollow that let in little light, like a cave, roofed with the rock as it had grown there, holy with the awe of an older time,
sentences.n: luminis exigui is a genitive of description hung on recessus: a recess characterised by having little light. fuerat is a pluperfect where English is content with “there was”, because the place existed before the moment being told. similis takes the genitive speluncae. nativus is “as born”, so nativo pumice says the roof is the rock itself and not masonry. religio here is not a system of belief but the binding awe that attaches to a particular place, and prisca dates it.

sentences.t:
quo multa sacerdos
lignea contulerat veterum simulacra deorum.
sentences.l: to which a priest had brought together many wooden images of the gods of old.
sentences.i: and a priest had gathered into it many wooden images of the old gods.
sentences.n: quo is the relative adverb of motion, “to which place”, so English wants “into it”. contulerat is a pluperfect again, keeping the images older than the scene. multa is split from the words it belongs with, lignea simulacra, across the line-end: multa stands second from the end of 693, lignea opens 694, and the noun simulacra comes only after the verb. Wooden images are the oldest kind, which is the point of veterum deorum standing at the end.

sentences.t: Hunc init et vetito temerat sacraria probro.
sentences.l: He goes into it and defiles the sanctuary with a forbidden shame.
sentences.i: He goes inside, and violates the holy place with an act of shame forbidden there.
sentences.n: Hunc picks up recessus from the sentence before. init is the present of ineo, which takes as its object the place gone into. temerare is the specific verb for violating what has been consecrated. probrum is a shameful act rather than a description of one: the poem names the deed only by the disgrace of it and says nothing else about what happened. vetito is what the place forbids, not the law generally. The judgment in the words is Venus's own, and she has just said that she stirred the desire that produced the act. Both verbs, init and temerat, are singular and have Hippomenes alone for their subject; Atalanta does not enter the sentence at all, and appears only inside the plural sontes at 697. sacraria is plural for singular.

sentences.t:
Sacra retorserunt oculos; turritaque Mater
an Stygia sontes dubitavit mergeret unda.
sentences.l: The holy images twisted their eyes away; and the tower-crowned Mother hesitated whether she should sink the guilty pair in the Stygian water.
sentences.i: The sacred images turned their eyes aside, and the Mother in her crown of towers wondered whether to drown the guilty pair in the water of Styx.
sentences.n: Sacra is the neuter plural of things consecrated — here the wooden images just described, which are given eyes to turn. turrita is the standing epithet of Cybele, who is shown wearing a crown shaped like a city wall. dubitavit takes an indirect question introduced by an alone, with mergeret in the subjunctive; an on its own for “whether” is ordinary in verse. sontes is the legal word for the guilty in a charge, and it is plural: the sentence has both of them in view. Stygia unda is an ablative of place with no preposition.

sentences.t: Poena levis visa est.
sentences.l: The penalty seemed light.
sentences.i: It seemed too light a punishment.
sentences.n: Four words on which the whole tale turns. levis is “light”, and the weight it is being measured against is the offence; since she rejects it, English wants “too light”. visa est has no dative of the person it seemed so to — the judgment is Cybele's, carried over from the sentence before.

sentences.t:
Ergo modo levia fulvae
colla iubae velant, digiti curvantur in ungues,
ex umeris armi fiunt, in pectora totum
pondus abit, summae cauda verruntur harenae.
sentences.l: So tawny manes veil necks smooth a moment ago, fingers curve into claws, forelegs come out of shoulders, the whole weight goes forward into the chest, the surface sands are swept by a tail.
sentences.i: So tawny manes cover necks that were smooth a moment before; fingers curve into claws; shoulders become forelegs; the whole weight goes forward into the chest; and the top of the sand is swept by a tail.
sentences.n: modo is “only just now” and goes with levia, so the smoothness is dated to the instant before. Five clauses follow one another with no connective at all, which is what the speed of the change sounds like. armus is the shoulder of an animal where umerus is the shoulder of a person, so the line changes the name of the part as the part changes. verruntur is passive with harenae, nominative plural, as its subject and cauda as the ablative of the instrument — the sand is swept, the tail sweeps it. Neither of the two is named anywhere in the sentence: the subjects are the body parts themselves — manes, fingers, forelegs, weight, sand — and the plurals among them cover both bodies at once without saying so.

sentences.t:
Iram vultus habet, pro verbis murmura reddunt,
pro thalamis celebrant silvas:
sentences.l: The face has anger in it; in place of words they give back growls; in place of a marriage chamber they haunt the woods:
sentences.i: Their faces hold anger; instead of words they answer with growls; instead of a bridal chamber they keep to the woods:
sentences.n: vultus is singular for the two of them. The two pro phrases do the arithmetic of the punishment, setting out what has been taken away beside what has been put in its place. thalamus is the marriage chamber, which is what duxit at 680 pointed to and what they have lost. celebrare is the verb for a crowd thronging a place at a festival, used here of two animals in a wood.

sentences.t:
aliisque timendi
dente premunt domito Cybeleia frena leones.
sentences.l: and, to be feared by everything else, they press Cybele's bit with a tamed tooth — lions.
sentences.i: and now, a terror to everything else, they champ Cybele's bit with a tooth she has tamed: they are her lions.
sentences.n: timendi is a gerundive, “to be feared”, with aliis as its dative of agent. leones stands last in the sentence and last in the tale, so the word that says what they became is the word held back to the end; the literal keeps it there. dente domito is the ablative of the instrument, and it is the tooth that is called tamed, not the beast — the tooth is on the goddess's rein. Cybeleia is an adjective formed from the goddess's name, and the sentence is an aetiology: this is where the lions that draw the Mother's car come from.

sentences.t:
Hos tu, care mihi, cumque his genus omne ferarum,
quod non terga fugae, sed pugnae pectora praebet,
effuge, ne virtus tua sit damnosa duobus.”
sentences.l: These, you, dear to me — and along with these the whole kind of wild beasts that offers not its back for flight but its chest for the fight — get clear of them, so that your courage may not be the ruin of two.”
sentences.i: Keep clear of them, my dear — of these, and of every kind of wild animal that will not turn its back and run but puts its chest into the fight — so that your courage does not destroy two of us.”
sentences.n: The objects come first and the imperative effuge does not arrive until the third line, so the warning is loaded before it is given; the literal keeps that order and English has to pick the sentence up again with “get clear of them”. terga fugae and pugnae pectora are datives of the purpose each part of the body is offered for, and they are set crosswise, back-flight, fight-chest. ne … sit damnosa is a negative purpose clause. duobus is “to two”, and the two are Adonis and Venus herself: she counts her own loss in advance. The quotation mark at the end of the line closes the speech she has been making, which began before this part.

sentences.t:
Illa quidem monuit iunctisque per aera cygnis
carpit iter:
sentences.l: She for her part gave the warning, and with her swans yoked she takes her way through the air:
sentences.i: She had given her warning; and with her swans harnessed she set off through the air:
sentences.n: The frame changes here: Venus stops speaking and the singer resumes telling the story about her, so she becomes illa, “she”, at the start of the line. quidem concedes the whole warning in one word and waits for the sed that undoes it. iunctis cygnis is an ablative absolute, a self-contained “with the swans yoked” where English wants a clause. carpere iter is the standing idiom for making a journey, literally to pluck one's way.

sentences.t: sed stat monitis contraria virtus.
sentences.l: but courage stands, set against warnings.
sentences.i: but courage stands its ground, against all warning.
sentences.n: stat is not merely “is” but the verb of standing firm, of a thing that holds its position; contraria takes the dative monitis. There is no possessive: the line does not say whose courage, and the reader has to bring Adonis to it. virtus is both courage and the quality of being a man, and the noun is feminine, so contraria agrees with it.

sentences.t:
Forte suem latebris vestigia certa secuti
excivere canes,
sentences.l: By chance dogs, having followed a sure trail, started a boar out of its hiding-places,
sentences.i: It happened that hounds, on a sure trail, put up a boar out of its lair,
sentences.n: forte again puts the whole scene down to chance. secuti is the perfect participle of the deponent sequor and is active in sense, “having followed”. latebris is an ablative of separation with excivere, out of the place the animal was lying in. excivere is exciverunt. The object suem stands near the head of the sentence, a line before excivere, the verb that governs it.

sentences.t:
silvisque exire parantem
fixerat obliquo iuvenis Cinyreius ictu.
sentences.l: and, as it was making to come out of the woods, the young man of Cinyras' line had struck it through with a slanting blow.
sentences.i: and as it was making to break out of the woods, Cinyras' young descendant had run it through with a blow from the side.
sentences.n: parantem is accusative and belongs to suem back in 710, the same boar being now the object of fixerat. silvis is another ablative of separation. fixerat is pluperfect, so the wound is put before everything that follows and the order of events is fixed by the tense alone. Cinyreius is a patronymic adjective; Adonis is not named in the sentence in which he wounds the animal, and is not named again until Venus speaks his name at 726.

sentences.t:
Protinus excussit pando venabula rostro
sanguine tincta suo trepidumque et tuta petentem
trux aper insequitur totosque sub inguine dentes
abdidit et fulva moribundum stravit harena.
sentences.l: At once it shook the hunting spear out with its curved snout, stained as the spear was with its own blood; and him, panicking and making for safety, the savage boar goes after, and buried its tusks entire beneath his groin and laid him down dying on the tawny sand.
sentences.i: At once it worked the spear out with its curved snout, the shaft wet with its own blood, and the boar came after him as he panicked and ran for safety, and sank its tusks their whole length under his groin, and laid him out dying on the yellow sand.
sentences.n: The subject acts for two lines before it is named: excussit has no expressed subject, and trux aper, “the savage boar”, arrives only in 715. venabula is the plural used of the one hunting spear or of several; tincta agrees with it, and sanguine suo is the boar's own blood, from the wound it is pulling the shaft out of. trepidum is an adjective and petentem a participle, both accusative and both of Adonis, who is given no noun of his own anywhere in the sentence. insequitur is a present set between the perfects excussit and abdidit. totos … dentes frames sub inguine, and moribundum, “dying”, is the object of stravit, which is the verb for laying a thing flat. fulva harena is the colour that runs through this part: the leaves and the gold at 648, the manes at 698, the mud at 733.

sentences.t:
Vecta levi curru medias Cytherea per auras
Cypron olorinis nondum pervenerat alis,
agnovit longe gemitum morientis et albas
flexit aves illuc.
sentences.l: Cytherea, borne in her light car through the middle of the air, had not yet reached Cyprus on swan wings; she caught, far off, the groan of the dying man, and turned her white birds that way.
sentences.i: Cytherea, riding her light chariot through the open air, had not yet reached Cyprus on her swans' wings when she caught, far off, the groan of a man dying, and turned the white birds towards it.
sentences.n: Latin sets the two clauses side by side with no connective — “had not yet arrived; she heard” — and English has to supply the “when”. Cypron keeps its Greek accusative ending. pervenerat takes the bare accusative of the place reached, without the ad the verb usually wants. olorinis alis is the adjective of the olor, the swan. agnovit is to know a thing for what it is, not merely to hear it. morientis is a present participle used as a noun, “of one dying”, with no name attached to it. albas and aves are split across the line-end, albas closing 719 and aves following its verb at the start of 720.

sentences.t:
Utque aethere vidit ab alto
exanimem inque suo iactantem sanguine corpus,
desiluit pariterque sinum pariterque capillos
rupit et indignis percussit pectora palmis.
sentences.l: And when from the high air she saw him without breath, and his body tossing in its own blood, she leapt down and tore alike her dress and alike her hair, and struck her breast with hands that had deserved no such thing.
sentences.i: And when she saw from high in the air that he had no breath left, his body rolling in its own blood, she sprang down; she tore her dress and tore her hair, and beat her breast with hands that had done nothing to deserve it.
sentences.n: ut with the perfect indicative vidit is “as soon as”. exanimis is “out of breath” as well as “lifeless”, and the second half of the line, where the body is still tossing, needs the first sense as much as the second. iactantem agrees with the same person and has corpus as its object, so the body is being thrown about by the man rather than lying still. sinus is the fold of the dress across the breast. pariter … pariter puts the two tearings side by side as one act. indignis is the standard Latin idiom for what does not deserve what is being done to it: the hands are innocent of the death and are being punished for it. Tearing the dress and the hair and beating the breast are the formal signs of mourning, and a goddess is here doing what mortals do.

sentences.t:
Questaque cum fatis “at non tamen omnia vestri
iuris erunt” dixit.
sentences.l: And, having made her complaint against the fates, she said: “Yet not everything will be of your jurisdiction.”
sentences.i: And she lodged her complaint against the fates: “Even so,” she said, “not everything will be yours to decide.”
sentences.n: questa is the perfect participle of the deponent queror, active in sense, and queri cum is to lodge a complaint against a party rather than to grieve in general. vestri iuris is a genitive of the thing something falls under — “of your law, of your right” — which is a phrase out of the courts, and both layers keep the legal colour rather than flattening it to “in your power”. vestri is plural: she addresses the fates as a body, and the at, “yet”, sets what she is about to do against what they have already done.

sentences.t:
“Luctus monimenta manebunt
semper, Adoni, mei, repetitaque mortis imago
annua plangoris peraget simulamina nostri.
sentences.l: “The memorials of my mourning will remain for ever, Adonis, and the image of your death, repeated, will carry through year by year the imitations of my beating of the breast.
sentences.i: “What keeps my mourning in memory will last for ever, Adonis: your death, played out again and again, will perform each year an imitation of my grief.
sentences.n: luctus and its possessive mei are split across the line-end, with monimenta manebunt semper and the vocative Adoni standing between them. plangor is the loud beating of the breast that Roman mourning consists of, and simulamina, a rare noun, is the imitating of it; peragere is the verb for carrying a rite through to its end. annua is an adjective doing adverbial work, “year by year”. nostri is the plural of a single speaker, as nobis will be at 730. The lines are an aetiology of the yearly mourning rite held for Adonis, which the poem describes without naming.

sentences.t: At cruor in florem mutabitur.
sentences.l: But the shed blood will be changed into a flower.
sentences.i: But his blood will be turned into a flower.
sentences.n: cruor is properly blood that has been spilt, as against sanguis, the blood inside a living body; the distinction is not being pressed here, since the same blood is sanguis at 721 and 735 and cruor at 728 and 731. mutabitur is a plain future passive, and in with the accusative gives the thing turned into. The change is announced before it happens, and by the goddess who will bring it about.

sentences.t:
An tibi quondam
femineos artus in olentes vertere mentas,
Persephone, licuit: nobis Cinyreius heros
invidiae mutatus erit ?” —
sentences.l: Was it allowed to you once, Persephone, to turn a woman's limbs into fragrant mint — and shall the hero of Cinyras' line, once changed, be for a grudge to me?”
sentences.i: You were allowed once, Persephone, to turn a woman's body into sweet-smelling mint: and shall it be grudged me if Cinyras' hero is changed?”
sentences.n: an opens an indignant question with no first limb stated, the effect being “or is it that …?”. licuit is impersonal, with tibi as the person permitted and vertere as the thing permitted. olentes is only “smelling”, and takes its sweetness from the plant it is attached to. invidiae is a predicative dative — “for a grudge” — paired with nobis, the construction grammars call the double dative; the grudge is one others would hold against Venus, not one she holds, and nobis is Venus herself, plural for singular again. The mint is Menthe, whom Persephone turned into the plant. The edition prints a space before the question mark, which is a feature of the printing and not a mark of anything in the text.

sentences.t:
Sic fata cruorem
nectare odorato sparsit:
sentences.l: — Having spoken so, she sprinkled the shed blood with scented nectar:
sentences.i: — So saying, she sprinkled scented nectar over the blood:
sentences.n: fata is the perfect participle of the deponent for, fari, “to speak”, and is active in sense: “having said”. spargere takes the accusative of the thing sprinkled on and the ablative of what is sprinkled over it, which is the reverse of the English idiom. nectar is the drink of the gods, used here as a liquid poured. The edition prints a dash where the speech ends and the telling resumes.

sentences.t:
qui tactus ab illo
intumuit sic ut fulvo perlucida caeno
surgere bulla solet.
sentences.l: and it, touched by the nectar, swelled just as a clear bubble is accustomed to rise out of tawny mud.
sentences.i: and at its touch the blood swelled, the way a clear bubble rises out of yellow mud.
sentences.n: qui is a connecting relative opening a new sentence and picking up cruorem, so English says “and it”; ab illo is the nectar. sic ut with solet is the plainest form a simile can take, “just as X is in the habit of doing”. perlucida is “see-through”, and it belongs to bulla, the bubble of the simile, not to the blood. Magnus prints tactus, “touched”; the second witness reads tinctus, “steeped”, which would make the nectar soak the blood rather than merely meet it.

sentences.t:
Nec plena longior hora
facta mora est, cum flos de sanguine concolor ortus,
qualem, quae lento celant sub cortice granum,
punica ferre solent.
sentences.l: Nor was the delay made longer than a full hour, when a flower rose out of the blood, of one colour with it, of the kind that pomegranates, which hide their seed under a pliant rind, are accustomed to bear.
sentences.i: It took no longer than a full hour: a flower came up out of the blood, its colour exactly, of the kind the pomegranate bears — the tree that keeps its seed under a supple rind.
sentences.n: plena hora is an ablative of comparison after longior. The sentence turns over on its cum clause again, as at 652: the delay is the grammatical subject and the flower arrives inside the subordinate clause. ortus stands with est understood. concolor is a compound adjective, “of one colour with”, and what it matches is the blood. qualem is drawn into the accusative as the object of ferre. punica are pomegranates, and lento cortice is the tough, pliant rind. The flower is not named here, and will be identified only by the wind that shakes it in the last line.

sentences.t:
Brevis est tamen usus in illo:
namque male haerentem et nimia levitate caducum
excutiunt idem, qui praestant nomina, venti.”
sentences.l: Yet the use of it is short: for the same winds that furnish its name shake it down, clinging badly as it does and ready to fall from too much lightness.”
sentences.i: Its season, though, is short: it holds on poorly, and is too light to stay, and the same winds that give it its name are what shake it off.”
sentences.n: usus is the enjoyment or use one gets of a thing rather than its beauty. male haerentem and caducum are accusatives agreeing with the flower, the object of excutiunt; nimia levitate is an ablative of cause with caducum, which is the adjective of a thing liable to fall. idem and venti are split around the relative clause qui praestant nomina, so the subject of the sentence is completed only by the last word of it. praestare nomina is to supply a name: the Greek word for wind gives the flower the name anemone, which the poem leaves for the reader to say. The quotation mark that closes the line shuts a quotation opened before this part — the song this whole tale has been sung inside.
